metaDescription: Six submersible sewage pumps compared on solids handling, motor size, cast iron build, float design and basin fit for basement baths and ejector pits.
expertTake: The Zoeller Waste-Mate 267 is the sewage pump to buy for a basement bathroom you cannot afford to lose, the Wayne RPP50 is the value pick with a big flow rating and a tether float, and the Superior 93020 is the easiest way to get a pump, basin and fittings in one box. Skip a sewage pump entirely if you only need to move groundwater, because a sump pump is cheaper and does that job better. Whichever you choose, the sealed lid, the roof vent and a sewage-rated check valve matter as much as the pump itself.
introParagraphs: A sewage pump has one job that a sump pump never has: it must move waste. That means passing solids without clogging, running long enough to empty a basin that fills with every flush and surviving a corrosive, grimy environment that would destroy a cheap pump in a season. The pump is the working half of an ejector system that lifts bathroom waste from below the sewer line up to it.

The decisions here are different from those in a sump pump guide. Solids handling, housing material, float type and basin size matter more than raw flow. A sewage pump that clogs once will clog again, and a failure here is a health problem, not just a wet floor.

products.name: Zoeller Waste-Mate 267-0001 1/2 HP automatic sewage pump
products.description:
The Waste-Mate 267 is the standard that other sewage pumps are measured against. It is a heavy-duty 1/2 HP automatic pump that passes 2 inch spherical solids through a non-clogging vortex impeller, operated by a float switch with a two-pole mechanical contact. That description reads as boring, and boring is exactly what you want in a pump that sits in a sewage basin.

The vortex design keeps the impeller out of the main flow path, so rags and solids pass without wrapping the blades. The 2 inch solids rating is the code-relevant spec for a residential ejector. Compared with the Liberty LE51A, also at 1/2 HP, the Zoeller costs more and does not claim a higher flow number; you are paying for the record, not the rating.

Ownership means checking the float and the lid seal yearly and having a plumber pull the pump if it ever hums without moving. It is built to run unattended for years. In year three, expect to touch it only to test the float and swap the check valve. The cord strain relief and the switch contacts are the wear items, and a plumber can pull the pump in minutes if the basin has a proper union connection. Because it also handles effluent and dewatering, it is a sensible choice if the basin may see both waste and groundwater.
products.bestFor: Basement bathrooms and ejector pits where reliability matters most.
cons: Costs more than imported cast iron pumps
Heavy to pull from a basin

products.name: Liberty Pumps LE51A 1/2 HP automatic submersible sewage pump
products.description:
The LE51A is a heavy cast iron automatic sewage pump with an oil-filled, thermally protected motor and permanently lubricated ball bearings. The oil carries heat from the windings into the cast iron housing, and the thermal protector shuts the motor down before it burns.

A 2 inch discharge is the standard for residential ejectors. The automatic float switch controls it without a separate panel. Compared with the Zoeller 267, the Liberty offers a similar class of build at a similar cost.

It is a dependable choice. Keep the basin lid sealed, check the float yearly and replace the check valve when it wears. A thermal protector is not a substitute for a clean basin, so keep grease and wipes out of the system, because the usual cause of a seized pump is a hairball of fibers around the impeller. Keep a record of the install date, since pumps in this duty are commonly replaced on a schedule of several years rather than run to failure.
products.bestFor: A cast iron sewage pump from a respected plumbing brand.
cons: Few published flow figures in the data

products.name: Wayne RPP50 1/2 HP cast iron sewage pump, 6,200 GPH
products.description:
The RPP50 is a 1/2 HP cast iron submersible sewage pump rated for up to 6,200 GPH with a piggyback tether float switch. It is designed for basins 18 inches in diameter or larger, which is the common ejector size.

The tether float swings on a cable, so it needs room in the basin, and the piggyback plug allows manual operation by plugging the pump straight into the wall. Against the Zoeller 267, the Wayne claims a high zero-lift flow at a lower price.

Treat the 6,200 GPH figure as a best case. Check that the float has space to swing and test it twice a year. Watch for a tether that is set too short, which makes the pump short cycle, and one set too long, which leaves waste standing in the basin. Adjust it so the pump runs a full cycle of a minute or two each time it starts.
products.bestFor: A value cast iron sewage pump for a standard 18 inch basin.
cons: Tether float needs room to swing
Zero-lift rating is a best case

products.name: Superior Pump 93020 1/2 HP cast iron sewage pump system with basin
products.description:
The Superior 93020 is a system, not just a pump: a 1/2 HP cast iron sewage pump with a vertical float switch, plus an 18 by 30 inch, 30 gallon structural foam basin with a 4 inch rubber inlet hub and a 2 inch discharge. It pumps up to 4,800 GPH and lifts water 25 feet.

The pump passes 2 inch solids with a non-clogging vortex impeller. Having the basin included saves sourcing parts and gets a basement bath running quickly, though it is a heavier package to move.

It is the easiest way to add a basement bathroom. Seal the basin lid, vent it properly and have the install inspected. Check that the inlet hub matches your pipe schedule and that the basin lid seals with the gasket supplied, since a leaking lid lets sewer gas into the house. Vent the basin to the roof according to code and include a cleanout so the line can be rodded.
products.bestFor: A new basement bathroom where you need the pump and the basin.
pros: Rubber inlet hub fits standard DWV pipe

products.name: AQUASTRONG 3/4 HP 7,000 GPH submersible sewage pump
products.description:
The AQUASTRONG has a 3/4 HP motor, a 7,000 GPH rating, a 33 foot maximum lift and a 2 inch NPT discharge that passes suspended solids. A tethered float and a piggyback plug give automatic and manual operation.

More motor means faster basin emptying and more margin against long discharge lines. It also means more startup current, so it wants a dedicated circuit. Compared with the Wayne RPP50 at 1/2 HP, it offers higher rated flow.

The brand has less sewage-pump history than Zoeller or Liberty, so check the warranty and test the float regularly. Its 33 foot lift rating is a shutoff head, not a working point, so expect much less volume at a long vertical rise. Put it on a dedicated GFCI circuit and make sure the wiring can carry the extra startup draw of a 3/4 HP motor.
products.bestFor: Long discharge lines and basins that fill quickly.

products.name: LANCHEZ 1 HP 6,600 GPH cast iron sewage pump
products.description:
The Lanchez is a 1 HP cast iron sewage and effluent pump with a PSC copper motor and an adjustable tethered float. A cast iron casing cools better and lasts longer than plastic.

Its 6,600 GPH rating is high, but the 1 HP motor draws substantial current. Against the Zoeller 267, it is a bigger motor at a lower price with less record.

Use it where you want a lot of motor on a budget, and check the warranty at purchase. The 1 HP motor can short cycle a small basin if the float is set too tight, so size the basin to the pump. A bigger motor in a small basin is a common installation mistake that wears out switches quickly.
products.bestFor: A budget 1 HP cast iron option.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A sewage pump must pass solids. The Zoeller 267 and Superior 93020 are rated for 2 inch spherical solids, the usual residential standard. A pump that only passes 3/4 inch is an effluent pump, not a sewage pump. Check the rating by checking the sphere diameter, not just the word sewage in the title. Many pumps sold as sewage or effluent pass far smaller solids and will clog on the first heavy load.

Vortex impellers like the Zoeller's keep blades out of the flow path. Grinder pumps cut solids but need more power. For most single-family ejectors, a 2 inch solids vortex pump is correct. A grinder pump is a different machine with a cutter and a smaller discharge pipe, used where gravity or ejector systems do not fit.

A 1/2 HP pump like the Liberty LE51A fits most residential ejectors. A 3/4 HP AQUASTRONG or 1 HP Lanchez gives margin for long lines but draws more at startup. A larger motor also raises the cost of the wire and breaker, so ask an electrician before upgrading from 1/2 HP. Also check that your panel has a spare breaker before ordering.

Cast iron carries motor heat into the basin and resists corrosion. The Zoeller, Liberty, Wayne, Superior and Lanchez all use it. Avoid thermoplastic for sewage duty. A cast iron pump is heavy, so plan for a lifting chain or rope and a union fitting that lets you disconnect without cutting pipe.

A tether float like the Wayne's needs room to swing in an 18 inch basin. A vertical float needs less. Confirm the basin diameter before you buy. Measure inside the basin, not the outside, and allow at least 2 inches of clearance around the float arc.

A sewage basin needs a sealed lid and a vent to the roof, and a check valve to keep waste from returning. A cheap pump in a poorly vented basin is a smell and a safety problem. The check valve should be rated for sewage, with a swing flapper that passes solids, not a spring valve that traps them. Install a union above the valve so it can be serviced without cutting pipe.

specDecoder.meaning: The largest sphere the pump passes, which sets clog resistance. Larger solids ratings reduce clog risk for sewage.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Zoeller 267 and Superior 93020 are rated for 2 inch. Check the listing for the word spherical.

specDecoder.meaning: A recessed impeller that creates a swirl instead of cutting waste.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Zoeller and Superior use one. Impeller wear is slow but real in gritty effluent.

specDecoder.meaning: A device that shuts the motor down when it overheats. It resets itself after the motor cools.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Liberty LE51A has a thermally protected motor.

specDecoder.meaning: A float on a cable that swings to switch the pump. A tether float is adjustable by moving its cable clamp.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Wayne RPP50 and AQUASTRONG need room.

specDecoder.meaning: A plug-through switch that allows manual operation. It lets you run the pump by hand for a test.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Wayne and AQUASTRONG include one.

howWeEvaluated.title: Solids handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked each pump's stated solids rating. The 2 inch spheres on the Zoeller and Superior set the standard. A pump that lists no solids rating was treated as an effluent pump.

howWeEvaluated.title: Build
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed cast iron against thermoplastic, and permanently lubricated bearings and thermal protection. Corrosion resistance mattered more here than in clean-water pumps. Cast iron scored above plastic for this reason.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor size
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared 1/2, 3/4 and 1 HP, and noted the extra startup current of the larger motors. We noted that 3/4 HP and 1 HP pumps need a dedicated circuit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Float and basin
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at tether versus vertical floats and the basin diameter each needs. A float that cannot snag in a standard basin scored higher.

howWeEvaluated.title: Brand record
howWeEvaluated.description: We favored makers with long sewage-pump histories over unknown imports. Parts availability and warranty counted too.

rows: Cast iron 1 HP on a budget
High flow at a modest cost

cards.label: Tether float
cards.text: The Wayne RPP50, AQUASTRONG and Lanchez use tether floats that swing on a cable. They need basin space but are adjustable.

cards.label: Vertical float
cards.text: The Superior 93020 uses a vertical float that needs less width.

howToChoose.note: Tether for roomy basins, vertical for tight ones.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A 2 inch solids rating, cast iron and a sealed, vented basin. A basement bath cannot tolerate a clog. Add a high-water alarm on its own circuit so you hear about a failed pump before the basin overflows.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Zoeller 267 and Superior 93020 are both rated for 2 inch solids.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: The pump serves a finished basement bath. The Zoeller 267 or Liberty LE51A are the safer bets.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: It is a secondary effluent pit. The Lanchez or Wayne are enough.

maintenance.why: Run water into the basin and watch the pump cycle. Also check that the alarm, if fitted, sounds. A stuck float is the most common failure in an ejector basin.
A leaking lid lets sewer gas into the home. Look for gasket cracks and a blocked vent screen.
A failed valve lets waste flow back.
Grease and sludge build up and jam floats. Have a plumber pump out the basin if sludge is thick.
A damaged cord in a basin is a hazard. Replace the cord if the jacket is cracked.

faq.a: A sewage pump passes solids and is built for waste. A sump pump only handles clean groundwater. Never use a sump pump for sewage. Sewage pumps pass solids and are rated for it, while sump pumps are rated for clean water.
It means the pump can pass a sphere up to 2 inches across, the common residential standard. Smaller ratings are effluent pumps, which are meant for septic tank outflow rather than raw waste.

faq.q: Do I need a grinder pump?
faq.a: Usually not for a single-family ejector. A 2 inch solids vortex pump is typical. Check local code. Grinder pumps are mostly used where a small discharge pipe is required.
Sewage work involves venting and gas. Hire a licensed plumber and check local code. Local codes may require a permit and an inspection for any ejector system.

faq.q: How long do sewage pumps last?
faq.a: Several years or more, depending on cycling and maintenance. Cast iron lasts longer. Do not flush wipes, which jam even rated pumps. Plan on replacing the pump on a schedule rather than waiting for failure, and keep a spare check valve and float on hand.

faq.q: What size basin do I need?
faq.a: Most pumps need an 18 inch diameter or larger basin. A smaller basin short cycles with a big pump.
